title: Education policy: some international perspectives
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou surveys recent reforms in Australia, the UK, the US, New Zealand and Canada and finds a convergent move toward the science of learning, systematic phonics and knowledge-rich curriculums. She then draws four conclusions from the survey. Her core claim is that skills-based curriculums share a theoretical flaw, resisting the breakdown of skills into smaller chunks, which shows up concretely in early reading and in assessment built on vague progression statements. She also argues that these reforms are bipartisan and that knowledge is not a right-wing cause. The piece leans on quoted official reports, but the framing and conclusions are the author's own and tie together a coherent evidence-based case for explicit, knowledge-rich teaching.
points: Reform in several countries is converging on phonics, knowledge-rich curriculums and the science of learning.
Skills-based curriculums fail because they resist decomposing complex skills into teachable parts.
Systematic synthetic phonics works because it breaks reading into smaller chunks, unlike balanced literacy or whole-word teaching.
Vague progression statements create bureaucratic, time-consuming assessment that teachers everywhere complain about.
Support for knowledge-rich, explicit approaches crosses political lines, undercutting the claim that it is a right-wing project.
quotes: Many of the countries / jurisdictions above have experimented with skills-based curriculums and are now realising that they do not work. Very different people - teachers, parents, politicians, journalists - from very different education systems are all independently acknowledging a similar problem. The major theoretical flaw with skills-based curriculums is their resistance to breaking down skills into smaller chunks.

One of the most important jobs of any education system is teaching students to read their native language. Systematic synthetic phonics is a highly effective method of teaching students to read English. It relies on breaking down the complex skill of reading into smaller chunks.

Another big practical way that skills-based curriculums fail is by setting up very bureaucratic and time-consuming assessment systems that require teachers to assess students against very vague progression statements like “can make insightful inferences about a variety of texts”. Again, these progression statements do not break complex skills down into useful and workable sub-units.

People sometimes want to assume that explicit instruction, knowledge-rich curriculums and the science of learning are part of a dark fascist plot, but this is just transparently not the case. Labour governments in Australia and the UK are in favour of phonics.

The Ontario Human Rights Commission is not typically associated with right-wing positions. Emily Hanford’s Sold a Story podcast was produced by public radio in the US. Ultimately, skills-based curriculums are a wrong turning in educational history, and people from across the world and across the political spectrum are waking up to that fact and trying to fix the problem.
